schools.summary: Gill allows the seventy to include grandsons.
Ellicott reconstructs the addressees from the versions and reads the letter as mocking irony; Keil and Delitzsch note only that the ruse worked.
Henry reads the challenge as upbraiding, and Ahab's numerous house as no protection against vengeance.

debates.question: Who were the letters sent to?

sides.position: The rulers of Samaria; "Jezreel" is an ancient error
holders: the Septuagint and Josephus (as reported by Ellicott)

sides.position: "And sent from Jezreel to the princes of Samaria"
Read "Israel" for "Jezreel"

1.pericope_label: Jehu's letter to the rulers of Samaria

schools.summary: Gill explains what the nobles saw in the letters and identifies the palace officer.

Clarke judges the surrender unconditional and already culpable; Wesley names the two governors.

themes: two kings stood not before him
4.pericope_label: The fearful answer of the city

schools.summary: Gill notes the point already gained and the nobles’ unhesitating compliance.
Ellicott times the deadline, lists the manuscript variants, and finds the historian’s judgement in his verb; Keil and Delitzsch summarise the order and its execution.
Henry asks how guardians could betray such a trust, and recalls their earlier obsequiousness to Jezebel.
Clarke argues from "come to me to Jezreel" that the letters went from Jezreel; Wesley divides the guilt between Jehu and the Samaritans.

debates.question: Can the order and the obedience be excused?

sides.position: Jehu justly required it, since the Lord of all lives had commanded it; the Samaritans wickedly obeyed
Cold-blooded wretches, the whole of them
The historian's own diction shows he did not sympathise; his interest is in Elijah's word fulfilled by Jehu's wickedness

debates.question: What does "the heads of the men your master’s sons" read?

sides.position: Omit "men"
holders: the Syriac, Arabic and Vulgate (as reported by Ellicott)

sides.position: Keep "men", marking that only male descendants were to die

holders: the Alexandrian Septuagint and four Hebrew manuscripts (as reported by Ellicott)

6.pericope_label: The second letter, and the seventy heads

schools.summary: Henry takes the words as an acquittal of the people and a comparative acquittal of Jehu himself.
Clarke reads the two heaps as calculated terror and the speech as another irony.
Ellicott glosses the messenger, the unique word for heaps, and the three possible senses of "ye be righteous".

debates.question: What does "ye be righteous" mean?

sides.position: Guiltless of these deaths, and so with nothing to dread
"Ye are just, and therefore will judge justly"
A question — are ye righteous? — meant to make the people share the guilt
A plain acquittal of the people before God and the world

outliers.note: He reaches for parallels outside Scripture, citing modern Persia and the fixing of traitors’ heads on London Bridge.

8.pericope_label: The heads at the gate, and "Ye be righteous"

schools.summary: Gill makes the verse a lesson in providence, the actors being only instruments.
Ellicott glosses the falling to earth and the emphatic clause about Jehovah; Keil and Delitzsch note the people looked quietly on.
Henry resolves it into God’s righteous judgement while denying that God is the author of any man’s sin.
Clarke infers that the nobles who beheaded the seventy died in their turn.

debates.question: What are Ahab’s "priests"?

sides.position: Court priests, of the kind the heathen kings kept
Secular counsellors or nearest servants
holders: Thenius (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: Domestic chaplains employed in the idolatrous services

themes: nothing of the word of the LORD falls
the great men and the priests

schools.summary: Gill supplies the errand to Samaria and reads the brethren as nephews.

debates.question: Should the opening verbs be transposed?

sides.position: Yes — read simply that he arose and came, with the Syriac

12.pericope_label: Beth-eked, and the brethren of Ahaziah

Henry has the forty-two appointed as sheep for the sacrifice and slain with solemnity.

14.pericope_label: Taken alive and slain at the pit

debates.question: What did the giving of the hand signify?

sides.position: A pledge of good faith; striking hands sealed a compact
Perhaps no more than a help up into the chariot

15.pericope_label: Jehonadab the son of Rechab gives Jehu his hand

schools.summary: Gill finds vainglory and a pharisaical spirit in the invitation.
Ellicott renders "look on at" and explains why Jehu wanted the orthodox party to see him; Keil and Delitzsch keep motive apart from law.

Clarke breaks into apostrophe against an ostentatious and murderous hypocrite.

debates.question: Was Jehu’s zeal genuine?

sides.position: Vainglory, hypocrisy and a pharisaical spirit
Boastful and done to be seen, though his inward state cannot be judged
The question of motive is separable from the lawfulness of the act

outliers.note: He abandons exposition for direct address, arraigning Jehu in the second person.

themes: see my zeal for the LORD
the calves at Dan and Bethel
16.pericope_label: "Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD"

debates.question: Can Jehu’s announcement be excused?

sides.position: No — manifestly false and designed to deceive; we must not do the least evil that the greatest good may come

17.pericope_label: Samaria cleared, and the prophets of Baal summoned

schools.summary: Gill explains the holy convocation and the keeper of the garments.

debates.question: What does "from one end to another" picture?

sides.position: The rim of a vessel — the house was brimful
From corner to corner
Head to head

debates.question: Whose wardrobe supplied the vestments?

sides.position: The temple of Baal’s, since his priests had their own sacred dress
Jehu’s palace, supplying festal attire
Neither — Jehu merely directs the priests to wear their own distinctive dress

20.pericope_label: A solemn assembly, a full house, and the vestments

schools.summary: Gill infers that Jehonadab was let into the secret.

sides.position: As a transitive — "the man that letteth escape any of the men"

a precaution that looked like reverence
23.pericope_label: Searching out the worshippers, and the eighty at the door

debates.question: Who offered the burnt offering?

sides.position: The priests of Baal
Jehu himself, in the character of an ardent Baal-worshipper

debates.question: What is "the city of the house of Baal"?

sides.position: The citadel or stronghold of the temple, rushed into from the court
A kind of holy of holies where the most sacred images were kept
The temple outbuildings, numerous enough to be called a city
The sacred enclosure of the temple

themes: as soon as he had made an end
the city of the house of Baal
25.pericope_label: The slaughter, and the citadel of the house of Baal

schools.summary: Gill takes the burned images for lesser deities or decorations and leaves Baal’s identity open.

Clarke refuses to soften what the temple became.

debates.question: Was Jehu’s extirpation of Baal religious or political?

sides.position: Objectively lawful but subjectively selfish; his keeping Jeroboam’s worship proves policy, not zeal
A real extermination of Baal, with the calves left standing beside it
A genuine destruction, at least for the present, and a type of God’s triumph over all the gods of the heathen

26.pericope_label: The pillars burned, the house made a draught house, and Baal destroyed

schools.summary: Gill reasons that the word came by a prophet and reports the Jewish guess.

debates.question: How far does the divine commendation reach?

sides.position: To the deed only, not the motives, as the following limitation shows
In part, and so far as is here expressed
To the deed, though whether Jehu acted from a good principle is justly questionable
It is qualified by the parenthetic verse about the calves

debates.question: Who brought the word to Jehu?

sides.position: A prophet, supposed by the Jews to be Jonah the son of Amittai
Perhaps Elisha

29.pericope_label: The calves of Bethel and Dan, and four generations

schools.summary: Gill applies the negligence to Jehu’s moral conversation and notes the irony of the timing.

debates.question: What does "began to cut Israel short" mean?

sides.position: To cut off part after part of Israelite territory

themes: took no heed to walk in the law
the LORD began to cut Israel short
31.pericope_label: Jehu not careful to walk in the law, and Israel cut short

schools.summary: Gill measures the reign and reports the chronicle formula.

Henry sees the brevity of the notice as a judgement on a king who took no heed to serve God.
Clarke asks whether God designed that his decree should be executed by such means.

sides.position: At the outset of the reign, during the internal troubles
